parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a railway station lost-property office to report a bag she left on a train.
script: Good afternoon, lost property, Carrow Bridge Station. Dale speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I hope you can. I left a bag on a train yesterday evening and I'm getting a bit desperate, to be honest.
Don't worry, we get a lot of calls like this, and we do get a lot of bags back. Let me open the form on my screen. Right. Can I take your name first?
Sorry, could you spell the surname for me?
Halvorsen. Lovely. And what's the best number to reach you on?
I'd give you my landline, but I'm having building work done at home and the phone has been disconnected, so please use my mobile. It's 07700 914 382.
07700 914 382. Thank you. Now, you said yesterday evening. That would be Monday, wouldn't it?
No, it was Tuesday. I was at a conference on Monday and I travelled home on Tuesday. Today's Wednesday, although it feels like a week ago.
Tuesday, right. And which train was it?
The one from Carrow Bridge to Wexcombe. Let me look at my ticket. Yes, it left at 5.52. The 5.42 was cancelled, so everybody piled onto the next one, and that's why it was so crowded.
5.52. That's useful, thank you. Do you remember which coach you were in?

That's the odd thing. I started off in coach E, but there wasn't a seat, so I walked along and found one in coach F, just by the luggage rack. I must have put the bag up on the rack and then walked off without it when we got to Wexcombe. I was on the phone to my sister, you see.
Coach F. All right. Can you describe the bag for me?
It's green. Quite a dark green, so in poor light it can look almost black. And it's a holdall, a canvas one with leather handles and a zip across the top.
A green holdall. And is there anything inside that would help us to identify it?

Yes. My camera, in a padded case. That's what I'm really worried about. It's a good one and it was a present. Apart from that, there's a pair of walking boots, a jumper and a paperback novel, nothing very valuable.
So the camera's the main thing. Does the bag have a name tag or anything like that on it?
No. I've been meaning to put one on for years.

Never mind. I've put all that on the form. What happens now is this. The train will have been checked at the end of the line, and anything handed in goes to our central depot. I'll send a request to the depot tonight, and they usually reply within 48 hours. If it's there, we'll ring you on your mobile.
And then I'd come and collect it from you? I work until six, so I'd have to come after that.
That's fine. We're open from half past seven in the morning until 8.30 in the evening, Monday to Saturday. On Sundays we close at 6, but I assume you'll be wanting it sooner than that.
Definitely. So 8.30 on weekdays, great. Is there a charge?
There's a handling fee, I'm afraid. For a bag it's 4 pounds 50. For bigger items, like bicycles or large suitcases, it's 10 pounds, but yours won't count as one of those.
That's fine. As long as I get the camera back, I'll pay anything!
Well, let's hope it turns up. Is there anything else you can remember about the bag, Ms Halvorsen? The brand, perhaps?
No, it's an old one and the label has worn off, I'm afraid.
No problem. That should be enough for the depot to go on. I'll be in touch as soon as I hear anything. Thanks for calling, and try not to worry.
Thank you so much. You've been really helpful. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A radio presenter explains the rules of a new recycling centre.
script: Good morning, and welcome to Borough Briefing. This week we turn to a subject that affects almost every household: the new recycling centre on Fernley Road, which opens to the public this Saturday. I visited the site on Tuesday, and I'd like to take you through what residents need to know, because there are quite a few changes from the old centre.

First of all, why a new centre at all? Many of you will remember the old site on Tanner's Lane. Some people think it closed because of the flooding two winters ago, and the flooding certainly didn't help, but the council says the real reason is simpler. It could no longer cope with the amount of waste arriving. On busy weekends the queue of cars stretched back to the main road, and the neighbours complained about the traffic. The new centre is almost three times the size, with room for around 40 vehicles at a time.

Now, the practical details. In the past, you had to show a recent utility bill at the gate to prove that you lived in the borough. That system has gone. This week every household will receive a plastic permit card through the post, and you simply show it to the camera at the barrier. If your card hasn't arrived by Friday, you can collect a temporary one from the council offices, and for that you will need a bill. But once you have your card, you won't need to book a time slot, except for vans, which I'll come to in a moment.

So which vehicles can use the centre? Cars and small trailers are welcome seven days a week. Vans and pick-up trucks, however, may only come on weekdays, and they must book a slot online in advance. This is so that trades people don't fill the site on Saturday and Sunday, when ordinary families are trying to get in. If you've hired a van for a house move, the same rule applies, so please plan ahead.

When you arrive, you'll find staff in orange jackets on the site. They won't carry your rubbish to the bays for you, but if you have something heavy or awkward, a fridge, say, or a mattress, they will lift it out of your vehicle, so please don't hurt your back trying to do it alone. They can also tell you where things go if you're not sure.

Opening hours are from 8 in the morning until 6 in the evening, every day. There was talk of closing on Mondays to save money, but that idea was dropped after protests. Another idea was to stay open late on Thursdays, because that's when most people shop in town. In the end, though, it's on Fridays that the centre will stay open until 8, because that's what the market traders and shift workers asked for. So remember: Friday evenings for late opening.

Which brings me to the bays, and this is where the biggest change is. The site is organised as a one-way loop, so you drive round from left to right. First, at the beginning of the loop, you'll find the green skips. That's where all garden waste goes: grass cuttings, branches, leaves. Please don't bring it in plastic bags, as the contents then can't be composted. Next, just beside them, there's a metal cage for small electrical items, from kettles and toasters to hairdryers and phone chargers. Large appliances such as fridges and washing machines are dealt with separately, at the staffed bay at the back.

Further along, you'll see the blue containers. Until now, these were for cardboard, but that has changed. Glass bottles and jars now go in the blue containers. Please take off the lids and put them in the metal bin, and there's no need to wash the jars, just empty them. Cardboard goes in the yellow containers, and it needs to be flattened, so bring a knife with you if you have lots of boxes. Plastic bottles, cans and cartons go in the red ones. I mention that because it's easy to mix up the red and yellow containers when you first visit.

Finally, at the end of the loop, there's something completely new: a re-use shop. Anything in good condition that you no longer need, such as clothing, books, toys and small pieces of furniture, can be left there, rather than thrown away. Volunteers sort the items and sell them from a small shop beside the exit, and the profits will go to a local charity. So if you've got old paperbacks cluttering your shelves, that is the place for them.

That's all from me about the recycling centre. If you have questions, the council's helpline is open all week, and I'll put the number on our website. Now, let's turn to the weather, and I'm afraid there's rain on the way.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student and his tutor discuss the proposal for his dissertation on urban foxes.
script: Come in, Jamal, and sit down. I've had a look at your proposal. Before we go into the detail, remind me how you came to choose urban foxes.

Well, I did a module on urban ecology last term and I enjoyed it, but I suppose the real reason is that I see foxes all the time. There's a family living under the shed behind my flat, and I often watch them from the kitchen window at night. I started wondering where they go and what they eat.
Good. A personal connection is a good starting point. It keeps you going when the work gets dull. Now, the title. You've called it Urban Foxes in Britain.
Yes, I thought that sounded quite impressive.

It does, but I'm afraid it's far too broad. You couldn't cover that in a lifetime, never mind in a dissertation of 8,000 words. It's not that it's badly worded. It's simply the scope. I'd narrow it to a single neighbourhood. You mentioned Marlow Heath. What about how urban foxes use private gardens in Marlow Heath?
That's much more manageable. Yes, I'll change it.
Now, methods. You've suggested walking round at night counting foxes with a torch.
Yes, I thought it would be simple, and cheap.

Cheap, yes, but I'm not convinced. You'd disturb the animals, for one thing, which changes their behaviour, and a person walking down a street at two in the morning will miss most of what's happening. Camera traps are better, because they record the animals without disturbing them, and they work all night.
I did think about those. They cost a lot more, though, don't they?
The department has eight that you can borrow, so cost isn't an issue, and the batteries last for weeks.

Then the problem is the gardens. The cameras would have to be in people's back gardens, and I'm not sure many people will want a stranger's camera there. Honestly, that's the part I'm most worried about.
It's a fair worry, and you'll need to plan it carefully. But there's something else you may not have thought of. You'll need approval from the ethics committee.
No, foxes are fine. It's because the cameras might capture images of people, residents or their children, not only foxes. Don't assume it's all about the animals.
I hadn't thought of that. How long does approval take?
About three weeks, so submit the form early. Now, the practical plan. How long would each camera stay in a garden?
I was thinking two weeks, so 14 days.
That's a long time to ask of a householder, and you'd cover fewer gardens. In 10 days you'd record the regular visitors very well, and you could rotate the cameras more often.
And how will you contact the householders? Not by knocking on doors, I hope.
I did think of that, but then most people are out in the daytime. I could write a letter to each house.
A letter is too formal, and people throw them away. A short, friendly leaflet through each letterbox, with a photograph of a camera and your contact details, works much better.
A leaflet, then. That makes sense.
Next, the photographs. You'll end up with thousands of them. How will you handle them?
I'd planned to buy some specialist software, but it's very expensive.
You don't need it. Sort everything in a spreadsheet. Date, time, garden number, whether there's a fox. It's low-tech, but it will do the job, and you'll understand your data better.
Brilliant. Thank you. One more thing. The proposal is due on Wednesday, isn't it?
It was, but the department office is closed on Wednesday for the building work, so the deadline has been moved to Thursday. Please don't leave it to the last minute, though.
No, I won't. Thursday. When should we meet again?
Next week, same time. By then I'd like you to bring a draft of the questionnaire for residents. Keep it short, ten questions at most, about whether they have noticed foxes and whether they feed them.
A draft questionnaire. Okay, I'll have it ready. Thanks very much, Dr Brennan.
You're welcome. Good luck with it.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer explains how honeybees tell each other where to find food.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about one of the most remarkable communication systems in the animal world: the way honeybees tell each other where to find food. For centuries, beekeepers had noticed that when one forager discovers a good patch of flowers, dozens of others arrive within an hour. But how did the others know where to go? The answer came from an Austrian scientist, Karl von Frisch, who spent decades watching bees, and who shared a Nobel Prize for his work in 1973.

Von Frisch began with a simple problem. How could he tell one bee from another? Bees look very much alike, and he needed to follow particular individuals. So he marked them with tiny dots of paint, in different colours and patterns, and he put out dishes of sugar water at different distances from the hive. When a marked bee found the sugar, he could see exactly what happened when she returned home.

What he saw was a dance. There are in fact two main kinds. If the food is close to the hive, a returning bee performs what is called the round dance. She runs in a small circle, first one way and then the other. This tells the others that there is food nearby, but not in which direction, so they leave the hive and search the area around it. Von Frisch originally thought the round dance was used for anything up to about 100 metres. Later work suggested a shorter range, and the figure usually given today is within about 50 metres.

For food farther away, the bee performs the waggle dance, and this is where the real precision lies. The dance follows a figure-of-eight pattern, with a straight run through the middle, during which the bee waggles her body rapidly from side to side. Two features of the dance carry the information. First, the length of the waggle run, that is, how long the straight part lasts, tells the others how far to fly. The longer the run, the greater the distance. You might expect the speed of the dance to be the clue, but it is really the duration of the waggle. Second, the angle of the straight run compared with the vertical shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun. If the bee runs straight upwards, the food lies in the direction of the sun. If she runs at 40 degrees to the right of vertical, the others fly 40 degrees to the right of the sun.

Now, there's a puzzle here. The dance takes place inside the hive, in complete darkness, on the vertical surface of the wax comb. So how do the other bees follow? They cannot see the dancer. What they do is crowd around her and touch her with their antennae. Those are the long feelers on the bee's head, and they pick up the vibrations and movements of the dance. In effect, the audience reads the dance by touch.

You may ask how the bees know what kind of flower to look for. The dance itself says nothing about that. The information comes from the dancer's body. She has been moving through the flowers, so she carries their scent, and she also shares small samples of nectar with the bees around her. The followers learn the scent and then search for it when they arrive in the right area.

There is another complication. The sun moves across the sky, so a direction measured against the sun today will be wrong an hour from now. Bees compensate for this. They adjust the angle of their dance as the day goes on, and the followers allow for the sun's movement on their way to the flowers. On cloudy days, when the sun is hidden, bees can still find its position, because they can detect polarised light. This is a pattern in the sky that is invisible to us, but it tells a bee where the sun is, even through a break in the clouds.

Not every dancer is equally persuasive. The quality of the food source matters. A bee that has found a rich source of nectar performs a vigorous dance, with many waggle runs and a lively pace, and she attracts a large audience. A bee that has found a poor source dances weakly, or not at all. In this way the colony shares the work of foraging according to what is most rewarding, without any central control.

Finally, bees use similar dances when a swarm needs a new home. Scout bees fly out to look for hollow trees and other suitable places, and each returns to dance for the site she has found. Over several hours, the dances for the better sites attract more and more scouts, and the others stop dancing. When roughly 20 scouts are present at one site at the same time, the swarm has in effect reached a decision, and the whole colony takes off together. It's a form of voting, and it's remarkably effective. Next week, we'll look at what this tells us about decision-making in larger groups.

passages.title: Penbray Community Hall: hire guide
paras: Penbray Community Hall is run by a committee of local volunteers and is available for hire by residents, clubs and businesses. This guide explains how to book and what to expect.

Rooms. The Main Hall seats up to 120 people and has a stage and a sound system. The Garden Room seats 30 and opens onto a small patio. The Meeting Room seats 12 and is popular for classes and committee meetings. A fully equipped kitchen can be added to any booking.

Charges. Hire is charged by the hour. The Main Hall costs 28 pounds an hour, the Garden Room 16 pounds and the Meeting Room 9 pounds. Residents of the Penbray parish receive a discount of 20 per cent on all rooms, and registered charities pay half price. The kitchen is an extra 12 pounds per booking. All bookings are subject to a refundable deposit of 50 pounds, which is returned within ten days provided that the hall is left clean and undamaged.

Booking. Requests should be made at least three weeks in advance, using the form on the hall noticeboard or by email to the booking secretary. A booking is confirmed only when the deposit has been received. If you cancel more than 14 days before your event, the deposit is returned in full; after that, 25 per cent is kept.

Rules. The hall must be vacated by 11 pm on weekdays and by midnight on Fridays and Saturdays. Hirers must not use nails, tape or adhesive putty on the walls. Alcohol may be served only if the hirer has a temporary events licence, and a copy must be shown to the caretaker on arrival. Children's parties are welcome, but a responsible adult must be present for every ten children. Smoking, including vaping, is not permitted anywhere in the building.

Setting up and clearing away. The time you spend setting up and clearing away counts as hire time, so please allow for it when booking. The caretaker, Mr Dalloway, will open the hall 15 minutes before your booking starts and can show you where the chairs, tables and cleaning equipment are kept. Chairs and tables must be returned to the storage room before you leave.

passages.title: Fairmeadow Library: borrowing an e-reader
paras: Fairmeadow Library now lends e-readers to members, so that you can try digital reading before deciding whether to buy a device of your own. Each e-reader comes preloaded with around 40 popular titles, including novels, travel guides and biographies. You may add further books from the library's online catalogue using the free wifi in any of our branches.

Who can borrow. E-readers are available to members aged 18 and over who hold a current library card. Members with unpaid fines of more than 5 pounds must clear them first. Young people aged 14 to 17 may borrow an e-reader with a signed consent form from a parent or guardian.

Loan period. The loan period is 21 days. A loan can be renewed once, for a further 14 days, unless another member is waiting for the e-reader. Renewals can be made online, by phone or in person. An e-reader that is returned late is charged at 50 pence per day, up to a maximum of 10 pounds.

Care and returns. Each e-reader is issued in a padded case with a charging cable, and these must be returned with the device. Please do not remove the protective cover from the screen. Devices should be returned to the front desk, not placed in the book return slot, which may cause damage. If an e-reader is lost or damaged beyond repair, the member will be asked to pay a replacement charge of 85 pounds. Normal wear and tear is not charged.

Your own reading. Books borrowed digitally disappear automatically from the device when the loan ends, so there is no need to delete them. If you wish to keep notes or highlights, you can email them to yourself before returning the device; the library clears all personal data on return. Staff are happy to show you how to use an e-reader at our drop-in sessions, held every Wednesday at 2 pm.

passages.title: Safety in the warehouse: rules for all staff at Dunmere Distribution
paras: A  Everyone who works in the warehouse, including temporary and agency staff, must complete the safety induction before their first shift. The induction takes about three hours and covers fire exits, first-aid points and the layout of the site. Staff who miss it will not be allowed onto the warehouse floor and must rearrange it with their supervisor.

B  Protective equipment must be worn at all times on the warehouse floor. This means a high-visibility vest, safety boots with steel toecaps and, in the loading bays, a hard hat. Gloves are provided free of charge from the equipment cage and should be replaced as soon as they become worn. Employees who arrive without the correct footwear will be sent home to collect it, and the time lost will be unpaid.

C  Forklift trucks may be driven only by employees who hold a current certificate issued by the company. Pedestrians must keep to the green walkways marked on the floor and never walk beneath a raised load. If you need to cross a truck route, stop at the yellow line, make eye contact with the driver and wait for a clear signal. Drivers must sound the horn at every blind corner and must not exceed 8 kilometres per hour inside the building.

D  Manual handling causes more injuries than any other activity in the warehouse. Before lifting a heavy item, assess its weight and shape. If it weighs more than 20 kilograms, use a trolley or ask a colleague to help. Keep your back straight, bend your knees and hold the load close to your body. Report any pain immediately, even if it seems minor; do not wait until the end of the shift.

E  Pallets must never be stacked higher than four levels, and heavier items must always be stored on the lower shelves. Aisles and fire exits must be kept clear at all times, and any boxes found blocking them should be moved at once or reported. Damaged pallets should be tagged with a red label and taken out of use.

F  Accidents and near misses must be reported to the shift supervisor immediately and recorded in the accident book before the end of the shift. A near miss is an event that could have caused injury but did not, such as a box falling from a shelf. Reporting these helps the safety team to find problems before somebody is hurt. Serious injuries must also be reported to the safety officer within 24 hours.

passages.title: Moving up: how to apply for an internal promotion
paras: Dunmere Distribution prefers to fill senior posts from within the company whenever possible. Vacancies are advertised on the staff intranet and on noticeboards for ten working days before they are advertised outside the company.
Who can apply. You must have completed at least 12 months' service in your current role and have no active disciplinary warning. Part-time staff are eligible on the same terms as full-time staff.

How to apply. Applications are made on form HR-7, available from the intranet or the personnel office. You should explain, in no more than 400 words, why you are suitable for the post, and give two examples of work in which you went beyond your job description. You must tell your line manager before you submit the form, although he or she does not need to sign it. Completed forms are sent to the personnel office, not to the manager of the department with the vacancy.

Selection. Candidates are shortlisted on the basis of the written application. Shortlisted candidates attend an interview with a panel of three people, one of whom comes from a different department. Applicants for posts that involve supervising others are also asked to give a short presentation of five minutes on a topic that is given to them a week in advance.

After the decision. All applicants receive written feedback within five working days of the decision, and unsuccessful candidates may ask for a meeting with a member of the personnel team. You may apply for no more than two posts at the same time.

passages.title: Keepers of the light
paras: A  For centuries, a lighthouse was a lonely building on a dangerous coast, and the person who looked after it was one of the most isolated workers in the country. Early lights were little more than open fires of coal or wood, burning in iron baskets on hilltops or towers. By the eighteenth century, oil lamps with reflectors had taken their place, but they still demanded constant attention. The wicks had to be trimmed every few hours, and the glass cleaned of soot, or the beam would fade within minutes. The keeper's first duty was simple: the light must never go out.

B  The keepers who did this work came from many backgrounds. Many were former sailors who knew what a wrecked ship meant to the families left behind, and some lighthouses were passed from father to son. In most countries the lighthouse service was run by a national or regional authority, which set strict standards. Keepers were chosen after an interview and a medical examination, and they had to be able to read and write, since a daily log was kept. They wore a uniform, and inspectors visited without warning to check that the brass was polished and the lenses spotless.

C  Life on a rock lighthouse, far out at sea, was especially hard. Keepers worked in teams of three or four, and at the most remote stations they lived together for weeks at a time. When bad weather stopped the supply boat, their stores of food, fuel and drinking water had to be stretched, and one northern station is recorded as having been cut off for seven weeks in a single winter. Tradition required the men to share the cooking, the cleaning and the night watches equally, but the records suggest that disputes were common. Some keepers kept cats or goats, and others took up hobbies such as model-making and sketching to pass the long hours.

D  Families, in contrast, lived at shore stations on the mainland or on larger islands, where the keeper's wife and children often shared the work. Wives trimmed lamps, and children carried water and learned to read the weather. Schooling was a problem, since the nearest school could be many kilometres away, and some authorities eventually paid a teacher to travel to the larger stations. The families usually grew their own vegetables in walled gardens, because fresh produce was difficult to bring across rough water.

E  The work changed with technology. In the nineteenth century, large lenses made of rings of glass concentrated the light of a single flame into a beam that could be seen more than 30 kilometres away. The lens turned on a clockwork mechanism driven by a falling weight, which the keeper had to wind up every few hours through the night. Paraffin vapour lamps replaced oil lamps and gave a brighter light, but they brought the danger of fire. By 1900, many stations also had a fog signal, a horn or a bell, which was sounded by hand whenever visibility was poor, and some keepers recorded working it for more than 60 hours without rest.

F  The first threat to the keeper's way of life came with electricity. Once a lighthouse was connected to a power supply, or fitted with a generator, the lamp could be lit by a switch, and the long hours of watching the flame came to an end. Automatic bulb changers, which swapped a burned-out bulb for a fresh one, removed another task. By the middle of the twentieth century, the authorities had realised that a light that looked after itself could be monitored from a distance, and that a keeper's salary and housing were costing far more than the equipment.

G  Automation spread slowly at first, then quickly. In some countries the last keepers left in the 1990s. Sensors measured the brightness of the light and the visibility; solar panels and batteries took the place of generators; and radio links reported faults to an engineer in a regional office. A single technician could now care for dozens of lights, visiting each only a few times a year for maintenance. Critics worried about safety, but the records show that the number of lights failing did not rise, and satellite navigation was already reducing the reliance of ships on the lights.

H  Today, many former lighthouses have a second life. Some are rented as holiday homes, others contain museums, and a few are run by volunteers who lead visitors up the spiral stairs. The old keepers' logbooks, with their short daily entries on weather, passing ships and repairs, have become valuable sources for historians and climate scientists, who use them to reconstruct the storms and sea conditions of the past. Perhaps the most lasting legacy of the keepers is something simple: a record, kept faithfully for generations, that the light was lit.
